passage: In the engineering hostel, Naveen had noticed things one at a time. The money Harish borrowed "till Friday" three Fridays ago. The way Harish's phone went face down whenever anyone walked past. The nights he paced the corridor at two, and the mornings he snapped at the mess staff. "Family stuff," Harish said when asked about the money. "Just tired," about the pacing. Naveen had rehearsed an angry speech. Instead, on Sunday evening, sitting on the hostel steps with two cups of tea, he said quietly, "Harish, I've seen you up at two most nights, and you seem really low. The money doesn't matter to me. You do. Is something going on with those betting games?" Harish stared at his tea for a long time. Then he said, "How long have you known?"

qa.q: What did Harish say when asked about the money?
qa.a: "Family stuff."

qa.q: Why did Naveen drop the angry speech he had rehearsed?
qa.a: Naveen was worried and cared more about Harish than the money, and sensed an attack would only make Harish hide more.

qa.q: What made Naveen's remark likely to be heard, and what could come next?
qa.a: It was calm, specific and caring, with a question instead of an accusation; next Naveen could help Harish reach a counsellor.

qa.q: What might Harish be feeling when he asks "How long have you known?"
qa.a: Harish likely feels exposed and ashamed, but perhaps also relieved that someone noticed without shouting.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing missing money, mood changes and vague excuses, and choosing a calm, specific, caring remark over confrontation.

subtype: Stage 4: Consequences and loss of control [Actor]
passage: The results list was pinned outside the college office in Bahraich, and Hafsa found her roll number in a column she had never been in before: supplementary. Rashmi squeezed her arm; Hafsa pulled away. Three weeks ago she had promised Ammi, her hand on Ammi's hand, that she had deleted the card game. She had. For four days. Then, alone on the roof one night, the itch came back so strongly that she reinstalled it before she could think. Now the fee money was gone, she had not answered Rashmi's messages in days, and every promise she made felt true when she said it and false by nightfall. Walking home past the sweet shop, Hafsa felt trapped inside her own hands.

qa.q: Which column was Hafsa's roll number in?
qa.a: The supplementary column.

qa.q: What does "trapped inside her own hands" suggest Hafsa feels?
qa.a: She feels ashamed and trapped, unable to keep promises even though she means them when she makes them.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Hafsa now?
qa.a: Telling Ammi or Rashmi the truth and getting help from a counsellor or de-addiction service, since willpower alone keeps failing.

qa.q: What might Rashmi be experiencing now?
qa.a: Rashmi is likely worried and hurt, with messages unanswered and comfort pulled away from.

grounding: Shows slipping grades, lost money and strained friendships, with failed attempts to stop and sincere promises to family breaking under craving.

subtype: Stage 5: Hitting a wall and denial cracking [Actor]
passage: The scooter lay on its side near the Lajpat Nagar flyover, one mirror snapped off. Tarun sat on the kerb with a scraped palm, a traffic policeman writing something down, and the smell of last night still on his breath at eleven in the morning. Dolma, his flatmate, arrived in an auto twelve minutes after his call. She didn't shout. She knelt, looked at his hand and said, "Your mother called me twice. She was crying." Something in Tarun gave way. All the lines he had used for a year, it's just weekends, everyone drinks, I'm fine at work, simply weren't there. "I'm scared, Dolma," he said. "I'm so tired of this." Dolma sat down on the kerb beside him. "Okay. Then today we tell her, and today we call someone who can help."

qa.q: Where did the scooter lie?
qa.a: On its side near the Lajpat Nagar flyover.

qa.q: What does Tarun's "I'm scared" show about this moment?
qa.a: His denial has cracked, leaving fear and exhaustion where the excuses used to be.

qa.q: Why does Dolma's reaction matter so much at this stage?
qa.a: The opening for honesty can close fast; her calm support and plan to call help today keep it open.

qa.q: What might Tarun's mother be going through?
qa.a: She is frightened and crying, calling Dolma twice without knowing if her son is safe.

grounding: Shows an accident and a mother's tears forcing honesty, denial giving way to fear and exhaustion, and a friend reacting supportively in that brief opening.

passage:
Monday night.
I did it. At 9 a.m., before I could talk myself out of it, I called the de-addiction helpline the doctor at the clinic gave me last month. A counsellor called back at noon and booked me for Thursday. She asked the questions I'd been dodging for two years, and I answered them.
Then the harder part. I told Bhavna didi. I'd planned a whole speech and forgot it. I just said, "Didi, I drink every night and I can't stop by myself." She put down her phone, came and sat next to me, and said, "Vishal, thank you for telling me. We'll go on Thursday together." No lecture. No "how could you". She cried a little, then made us both rice.
I feel scared and lighter at the same time. The counsellor said recovery isn't a one-person job. Tonight, for the first time, it doesn't feel like one.

qa.q: When is Vishal's appointment?
qa.a: On Thursday.

qa.q: How does Vishal feel after telling Bhavna didi?
qa.a: Vishal feels scared and lighter at the same time, and less alone.

qa.q: What did Bhavna's reply do right?
qa.a: She thanked Vishal, offered to go on Thursday together and gave no lecture: support without shame.

qa.q: What might Bhavna be feeling when she cries a little?
qa.a: She may be sad and shaken by the news but also relieved to be told, and she chooses to stay steady for Vishal.

grounding: Shows a person telling a safe family member and contacting a counsellor through a helpline, and the family offering support without shame.

passage: The night Ojas told us, I was angry first. Four years of excuses, the missing gold chain, the lies about night shifts, and I had defended him to our parents every single time. Then guilt came right behind it: I'm his elder sister, I lived with him, how did I not see? And under both, strangely, relief. At least now it had a name. The counsellor at the de-addiction centre met our family on Saturday and said something I keep repeating to myself: "Dolma, this is an illness that can be treated, not a character flaw, and families need support too." So now I go to a family group on Wednesdays. Some weeks I still feel furious. But I no longer carry all of it alone, and when Ojas calls, I can answer without my voice shaking.

qa.q: On which day does Dolma go to the family group?
qa.a: On Wednesdays.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Dolma have the night Ojas told the family?
qa.a: Dolma felt angry, then guilty for not seeing it, and underneath both, relieved that it finally had a name.

qa.q: What has helped Dolma stay steady?
qa.a: Learning that the addiction is an illness that can be treated, not a character flaw, and joining a family group for support.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ojas when Dolma answers calmly?
qa.a: Ojas may feel less judged and more hopeful, hearing a steady voice instead of anger.

grounding: Shows a family member hearing the truth with anger, guilt and relief at once, then steadied by learning it is a health problem and getting support.

passage: Week eleven. Bilal's alarm went at 6:30, same as every day now, and he made his bed before he could argue with himself. Structure, his counsellor at the Hamburg clinic had said. Boring is good. Some days boring felt like peace. Other days it felt like sand in his teeth. On Friday evening his old football friends messaged: "Pub at eight, like old times?" His hands actually itched. He snapped at his sister Mina over nothing, then apologised. Instead of going, he walked the long way round the harbour, called Mina back and told her the truth: "It's a craving night." She stayed on the phone while he bought a falafel and walked home by a different route, away from the bar street. At ten he texted his counsellor their agreed check-in word: "Steady."

qa.q: What time does Bilal's alarm go now?
qa.a: At 6:30, same as every day.

qa.q: What was Bilal feeling when the old friends' message arrived?
qa.a: He felt a strong craving, his hands itching, and was irritable enough to snap at Mina.

qa.q: Which steps carried Bilal through the Friday evening?
qa.a: Telling Mina honestly it was a craving night, walking home away from the bar street and sending the check-in word to his counsellor.

qa.q: What is it like for Mina on the phone that night?
qa.a: Mina stays on the call, perhaps anxious but glad he told her the truth instead of going.

grounding: Shows early recovery with cravings, boredom and irritability, carried by routine, honest check-ins and avoiding old settings.

subtype: Stage 8: Relapse as a setback, not the end [Response]
passage: Eight months without tobacco, and last Saturday at my cousin's engagement I took a packet from an old friend in the parking lot. I felt the old rush, and then a cold drop in my stomach. The old me would have hidden it, told myself the eight months were wasted, and bought my own packet the next day. Instead I stood behind the tent and called Ramesh, my brother, who has driven me to every clinic appointment. My voice was shaking. "Ramesh, I slipped." He didn't sigh. He said, "Okay. Thank you for telling me. Where are you? I'm coming." On Monday I told my counsellor too. We looked at what happened: the crowd, the old friend, the parking lot. One lapse, not the end. I'm Harish, and I'm on day three again.

qa.q: Where was Harish when calling Ramesh?
qa.a: Behind the tent at the cousin's engagement.

qa.q: What did Harish feel right after the lapse?
qa.a: Harish felt the old rush and then a cold drop of fear and shame.

qa.q: What choice protected Harish's recovery?
qa.a: Telling Ramesh the same evening and the counsellor on Monday, instead of hiding the lapse.

qa.q: Why does Ramesh's reaction matter?
qa.a: His calm thanks and offer to come carry no punishment, which eases the shame that could have pushed Harish back to regular use.

grounding: Shows a person in recovery telling support people quickly after a lapse and returning to care, met with a kind, non-punishing reaction.

subtype: Stage 8: Relapse as a setback, not the end [Actor]
passage: The morning after the office party in Lisbon, Sofia woke with a dry mouth and the memory of wine she had promised herself she would never drink again. A hundred and forty days, gone. She sat on the edge of the bed. The thought came smooth and reasonable: You've already failed. Might as well stop pretending. There was a bottle shop two streets away that opened at ten. She noticed how kind the thought sounded, and how much it felt like the voice that had kept her drinking alone for years. That's shame talking, she remembered Elif saying at group. She picked up the phone. "Elif, I drank last night. And this morning I want to give up." "Thank you for calling," Elif said. "Meet me at the café at ten, not the shop. We'll call your counsellor together."

qa.q: How many days had Sofia gone without drinking before the party?
qa.a: A hundred and forty days.

qa.q: Why does the thought "You've already failed" feel so tempting to Sofia?
qa.a: She feels ashamed after the lapse, and the thought sounds reasonable and kind, offering an end to that painful feeling.

qa.q: What stopped the slip from becoming a return?
qa.a: Sofia recognised the thought as shame talking and called Elif that same morning, agreeing to meet and call the counsellor.

qa.q: What is it like for Elif to get Sofia's call?
qa.a: Elif seems glad to be trusted and steady, thanking Sofia and turning the morning toward help instead of the shop.

grounding: Shows the pull to give up entirely after a lapse, the thought recognised as shame, and a support person called that same day.

subtype: Stage 1: Task feels big or dull [Actor]
passage: Freya put the blank poster board on the kitchen table in Glasgow and stared at it. "Volcanoes," the teacher's sheet said. "Include a diagram, three facts and a picture." It looked enormous. Her tummy did a small flip, the same one she got before swimming lessons. She picked up a pencil, drew half a triangle, and stopped. Maybe she needed a snack first. She got a biscuit. Then she noticed her cousin Priscila's comic lying on the sofa and read two pages, just to see what happened. Then the cat wanted stroking. When Mum called from upstairs, "How's the volcano going?", Freya looked at the half triangle and felt the flip again.

qa.q: What did the teacher's sheet ask Freya to include?
qa.a: A diagram, three facts and a picture.

qa.q: What was Freya feeling when she stared at the blank poster board?
qa.a: She felt a small wave of dread, a tummy flip like before swimming lessons, because the task looked enormous.

qa.q: What small step could help Freya start?
qa.a: Finishing just the triangle diagram, or writing one fact, would make the big poster feel smaller.

qa.q: What might Mum be picturing when she asks about the volcano?
qa.a: Mum may imagine Freya busy working, not knowing she has drifted to a biscuit, a comic and the cat.

grounding: Shows a child facing a big project, feeling a small wave of dread and drifting to easier things like a snack and a comic.

passage:
"Ojas, forty minutes and you've written two lines!" Kamal stood in the doorway. "Such a lazy boy."
Ojas kept his eyes on the notebook. "I'm lazy," he said flatly. "Everyone says."
"I didn't mean..." Kamal stopped. "Who's everyone?"
"You. Dadi. Ma'am wrote it in my diary." He pushed the notebook away. "Lazy people can't do essays."
Kamal pulled up a chair. "Okay. What's the essay?"
"My Favourite Festival. Two pages."
"Two pages is too big to look at. Let's do one piece. Which festival?"
"Onam."
"What's the first thing you see on Onam morning?"
"The pookalam. Amma's flowers."
"Write just that sentence. I'll sit here."
Ojas wrote it. Then another. "Papa, don't go."
"I'm right here."

qa.q: What is the title of Ojas's essay?
qa.a: My Favourite Festival.

qa.q: What does Ojas's "I'm lazy, everyone says" reveal about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels hurt and discouraged, and now believes being lazy is simply a fact about himself.

qa.q: What does Kamal switch to that works better than scolding?
qa.a: He sits nearby and breaks the essay into one small piece, the first thing Ojas sees on Onam morning.

qa.q: What might Kamal feel when Ojas repeats "I'm lazy"?
qa.a: Kamal seems shaken and regretful, stopping mid-sentence on hearing his own word coming back.

grounding: Shows a child who has been called lazy starting to believe it, and a parent helping more by breaking the task down and sitting nearby.
